x: A zero-dependency React library for virtual-scrolling **waterfall (masonry)** and **equal-height** layouts, with infinite scroll and layout switching driven by your API. Features Virtual scrolling – only items near the viewport are rendered, so very long lists stay fast. Waterfall layout – Pinterest style, each item goes to the shortest column. Equal-height layout – Google Photos style, every row has the same height and each image keeps its aspect ratio. Dynamic layout – let the first API response decide which of the two layouts is used. Infinite scroll – built on IntersectionObserver with a configurable preload distance; only one page request is in flight at a time. Responsive – the container width is observed, columns and rows are recomputed when it changes. Written in TypeScript, with a peer dependency on React 16.8 or newer and no other dependencies. Installation Shell npm install react-hybrid-masonry # or yarn add react-hybrid-masonry # or pnpm add react-hybrid-masonry Quick start All three components share one contract: loadData(page, pageSize) returns { data, hasMore } , every item has a width and a height, and renderItem draws an item at the position the library computed. TSX import { VirtualMasonry } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; export function Gallery ( ) { const loadData = async ( page : number , pageSize : number ) => { const res = await fetch ( "/api/images?page=" + page + "&size=" + pageSize ) ; const json = await res . json ( ) ; return { data : json . items , hasMore : json . hasMore } ; } ; return ( < VirtualMasonry loadData = { loadData } pageSize = { 30 } minColumnWidth = { 200 } maxColumnWidth = { 350 } gap = { 16 } renderItem = { ( item ) => ( < div key = { item . id } style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height } } > < img src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" } } /> </ div > ) } /> ) ; } Which component should I use? Component Layout Use it for VirtualMasonry Waterfall: equal-width columns, items of different heights Image walls, product feeds, cards of different heights FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry Rows of equal height that fill the full width Photo albums, timelines, search results made of images DynamicMasonryView Either of the two, chosen at runtime When the back end or the content decides how a list is shown The data contract The components need the size of every item to compute its place before the image has loaded. The size is read from the first of these field pairs that exists: width / height , w / h , imgW / imgH . For any other shape pass mapSize : TSX < VirtualMasonry mapSize = { ( raw ) => ( { width : raw . cover . w , height : raw . cover . h } ) } /* ... */ / > Every item handed to renderItem is your original object plus the computed x , y , width and height (and widthRatio ). Your own fields such as url or title are preserved. The render contract The root element returned by renderItem must be absolutely positioned with the given left , top , width and height . Set a stable key (for example item.id ) on that element. In the waterfall layout the index argument counts only the items currently rendered and changes while scrolling. The components scroll with the window , not with an inner container. See the FAQ . Next: read the page for the component you picked, or jump to the pagination guide .

h.t: How the column count is chosen

x: Pinterest style waterfall layout: equal-width columns, items keep their aspect ratio and are placed into the shortest column. Only items near the viewport are rendered. Usage TSX import { VirtualMasonry } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; < VirtualMasonry loadData = { loadData } pageSize = { 30 } minColumnWidth = { 200 } maxColumnWidth = { 350 } gap = { 16 } renderItem = { ( item ) => ( < div style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height , } } > < img src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" } } /> </ div > ) } /> Props Prop Type Default Description loadData (page, pageSize) => Promise<{ data: any[]; hasMore: boolean }> – Loads one page. Page numbers start at 1. Without it the component stays empty. renderItem (item, index) => ReactNode required Renders one item. index is the position among the currently rendered items. pageSize number 50 Items requested per page. minColumnWidth number 200 Minimum column width in px. The calculated column count never makes columns narrower than this. maxColumnWidth number – Maximum column width in px. columns number – Fixed column count. Skips the width based calculation. gap number 16 Gap between items, horizontally and vertically, in px. buffer number 1500 Extra distance in px above and below the viewport that is still rendered. loadMoreThreshold number 800 Distance in px from the bottom at which the next page is requested. mapSize (raw) => { width, height } – Maps your data to dimensions. See the data contract . initialItems any[] – A first page you already have (for example from SSR). Page 1 is not requested again; loading continues at page 2. initialHasMore boolean true Used with initialItems : whether more data exists after the first page. enableAnimation boolean true Reserved. It has no effect yet. How the column count is chosen If columns is set, it is used as is. Otherwise floor(containerWidth / minColumnWidth) columns are used, at least 1. If maxColumnWidth is set and the columns would be wider than that, columns are added one by one (up to 20) until they fit, but a column is not added when it would make columns narrower than minColumnWidth . When both limits cannot be met, the minimum wins. The column width is (containerWidth - gap * (columns - 1)) / columns , capped at maxColumnWidth . When the cap applies, the grid is left aligned and the remaining space stays empty on the right. An item's height is columnWidth * (height / width) of its original size, and it is placed into the column that is currently the shortest. Examples Fixed number of columns TSX < VirtualMasonry columns = { 4 } gap = { 12 } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> Pick the number per breakpoint with a small hook, see responsive layouts . Start from data you already have TSX < VirtualMasonry initialItems = { firstPage . items } initialHasMore = { firstPage . hasMore } loadData = { loadData } // first call will be page 2 renderItem = { renderCard } /> Item sizes in other fields TSX < VirtualMasonry mapSize = { ( raw ) => ( { width : raw . imgW , height : raw . imgH } ) } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> Related: pagination and infinite scroll , performance tuning .

h.t: Choosing between this and the waterfall

x: A Google Photos style layout: images keep their aspect ratio, every row has the same height, and rows are scaled to fill the container width exactly. Only the rows near the viewport are rendered. Overview FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry lays images out row by row: every row has the same height and ends at the right edge, and every image keeps its own aspect ratio . How many images fit in a row follows from their proportions rather than from a fixed number of columns, which makes it a good fit for photo albums, timelines and search results where the images are the content. Layout for a 640px container with a 90px target row height and 6px gap (4 rows, the numbers are the image aspect ratios). Solid rows end at the right edge; the dashed last row keeps its natural proportions and is not stretched. All rows have the same height, and the gap between rows and between images is gap . Each image keeps its aspect ratio, with only a small deviation, see how the options work together . Only rows within buffer pixels of the viewport are rendered, so thousands of images do not slow the page down. The next page is requested as the user nears the bottom, with a single request in flight at a time. Quick start TSX import { FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; type Photo = { id : number ; url : string ; title : string ; width : number ; height : number } ; async function loadData ( page : number , pageSize : number ) { const res = await fetch ( "/api/photos?page=" + page + "&size=" + pageSize ) ; const json = await res . json ( ) ; return { data : json . items as Photo [ ] , hasMore : json . hasMore as boolean } ; } export function PhotoAlbum ( ) { return ( < FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry loadData = { loadData } pageSize = { 30 } targetRowHeight = { 245 } sizeRange = { [ 230 , 260 ] } gap = { 8 } renderItem = { ( item ) => ( < div key = { item . id } style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height } } > < img src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } loading = " lazy " style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" , display : "block" } } /> </ div > ) } /> ) ; } Every item needs a width and a height before it loads: the component computes positions from them instead of waiting for the images to download. See data and sizes below. Data and sizes Where sizes come from The size of each item is read from the first pair of fields that exists: width / height , w / h , imgW / imgH . Use mapSize when your data is shaped differently: TSX < FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry mapSize = { ( raw ) => ( { width : raw . cover . w , height : raw . cover . h } ) } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> Internally the component turns width / height into a widthRatio per image, and the whole layout depends on that ratio only, so any unit works: pixels, or plain ratio values such as 4 and 3 . Items without valid sizes cannot be laid out: a missing width or height gives NaN and every position in that row breaks. If the API may omit fields, give mapSize a fallback, for example { width: raw.w || 4, height: raw.h || 3 } . What renderItem receives The item passed to renderItem(item, index) is your original object plus the fields below, calculated by the layout. Your own fields ( url , title , ...) are kept: Field Meaning x Distance from the left edge of the container (px). y Distance from the top of the container (px). width Laid-out width (px). It replaces the width in your data . height Laid-out height (px), the same for every image in a row. It also replaces the height in your data . widthRatio The aspect ratio width / height . index is the position of the item among all loaded data . It stays the same while scrolling, so it is safe to use for a key or for tracking. To keep the original dimensions, have your API use other field names such as w / h and read them through mapSize . Rendering cards The root element you return must be absolutely positioned with the left , top , width and height you receive. Give the root element a stable key , such as item.id . Use object-fit: cover on images. To make each row end exactly at the edge an image's ratio can deviate slightly, and cover turns that deviation into a sliver of cropping instead of distortion. Put captions on top of the image. The layout decides the row height, so there is no extra space below an image. TSX const Card = React . memo ( function Card ( { item } : { item : Photo & { x : number ; y : number ; width : number ; height : number } } ) { return ( < figure className = " card " style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height , margin : 0 } } > < img src = { item . url } alt = { item . title } loading = " lazy " style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" , display : "block" } } /> < figcaption className = " card-caption " > { item . title } </ figcaption > </ figure > ) ; } ) ; // .card { overflow: hidden; border-radius: 6px; } // .card-caption { position: absolute; inset: auto 0 0 0; padding: 24px 12px 10px; opacity: 0; transition: opacity .2s; // background: linear-gradient(to top, rgba(0,0,0,.6), transparent); color: #fff; } // .card:hover .card-caption { opacity: 1; } While the width stays the same the layout result is stable, and visible items keep the same object reference as you scroll, so wrapping the card in React.memo avoids re-rendering it on scroll, see performance tuning . Props Prop Type Default Description loadData (page, pageSize) => Promise<{ data: any[]; hasMore: boolean }> – Load one page of data. Pages start at 1. renderItem (item, index) => ReactNode required Render one positioned item. index is its position among all loaded data. pageSize number 50 Number of items requested per page. targetRowHeight number 245 Target row height; decides how many images go into a row. The actual height is adjusted within sizeRange . sizeRange [number, number] [230, 260] Allowed row height [min, max] . maxItemWidth number 975 Maximum width of a single item. maxStretchRatio number 1.5 A row keeps taking images until filling it needs an enlargement no greater than this value. Shrinking is not limited. gap number 8 Horizontal and vertical space between items (px). buffer number 1500 Extra distance above and below the viewport that is still rendered (px). loadMoreThreshold number 500 How far from the bottom (px) the next page is requested. mapSize (raw) => { width, height } – Map your data to a width and height. enableAnimation boolean true Reserved, currently has no effect. This component currently has no initialItems / initialHasMore ; the first page is loaded through loadData after mounting. When you need full control of the data, use the Core component below. How the options work together targetRowHeight and sizeRange The two options do different jobs. targetRowHeight decides how many images go into a row : the component uses it to compute each image's ideal width and keeps adding images until filling the row needs an enlargement no greater than maxStretchRatio . sizeRange decides the final row height limits : the height needed to fill the row is clamped into this range, and then the image widths are distributed proportionally so the row ends exactly at the container edge. Target row height 50px: 3 rows, more images per row. Target row height 100px: 5 rows, fewer images per row. To make images larger overall, raise targetRowHeight and sizeRange together. If you raise only one of them, the other pulls the row height back. maxStretchRatio It controls how much a row is willing to enlarge its images. A smaller value makes a row take more images before it ends, so images are enlarged less; a larger value ends rows earlier with fewer images that are enlarged more. Shrinking is not limited. maxStretchRatio 1.5: 4 rows. maxStretchRatio 1.2: 3 rows, denser rows overall. maxItemWidth The width limit of a single image. A very wide

h.t: Three ways to pick the layout

x: One component, two layouts. The layout is controlled by a prop, by the first API response, or by a default. Three ways to pick the layout 1. Controlled TSX < DynamicMasonryView isMasonry = { useWaterfall } // true = waterfall, false = equal-height loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { ( item , index , isMasonry ) => /* ... */ null } /> The prop has priority over everything else. When it changes the active layout is remounted and loads from page 1 again. 2. From the first API response TSX < DynamicMasonryView loadData = { async ( page , pageSize ) => { const res = await fetch ( "/api/content?page=" + page + "&size=" + pageSize ) ; const json = await res . json ( ) ; return page === 1 ? { data : json . items , hasMore : json . hasMore , isMasonry : json . layoutType === "waterfall" } : { data : json . items , hasMore : json . hasMore } ; } } renderItem = { ( item , index , isMasonry ) => /* ... */ null } /> The component calls loadData(1, pageSize) once on mount, reads isMasonry from the result and caches that first page, so the chosen layout shows it right away and page 1 is not requested a second time. The layout type is read only once ; later pages do not need to return it. 3. Default value If loadData does not return isMasonry , defaultIsMasonry (default true ) is used. If the first request fails, onError is called and the default layout is used. Props Prop Type Default Description isMasonry boolean – Controlled mode. true = waterfall, false = equal-height. defaultIsMasonry boolean true Used when loadData does not return isMasonry . loadData LoadDataFn – (page, pageSize) => Promise<{ data, hasMore, isMasonry? }> . renderItem (item, index, isMasonry) => ReactNode required Render function. The last argument tells which layout is active. waterfallConfig { minColumnWidth, maxColumnWidth, columns, gap, buffer } {} Forwarded to VirtualMasonry . equalHeightConfig { targetRowHeight, sizeRange, maxItemWidth, maxStretchRatio, gap, buffer } {} Forwarded to FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry . pageSize number 50 Items requested per page. mapSize (raw) => { width, height } – Maps your data to dimensions. renderInitialLoader () => ReactNode empty block Shown while the layout type is being determined. onLayoutTypeLoaded (isMasonry: boolean) => void – Called once the layout type is known. onError (error: Error) => void – Called when the first request fails. enableAnimation boolean true Reserved. It has no effect yet. Exported types TSX import { DynamicMasonryView , ViewType , // enum: ViewType.Waterfall = 1, ViewType.EqualHeight = 2 } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; import type { DynamicMasonryViewProps , LoadDataFn } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; loadData is declared as LoadDataFn<T> ; only the first call may include isMasonry . Related: pagination and infinite scroll .

How pages are requested, when the next one starts, what happens on errors and how to start over. The loadData contract TSX type LoadData = ( page : number , // starts at 1 and increases by 1 for every successful request pageSize : number , ) => Promise < { data : any [ ] ; hasMore : boolean } > ; The component keeps all loaded items. Return only the new page from loadData ; the library appends it. Page numbers are tracked inside the component, you do not have to count them. When the next page starts A 1px marker sits at the bottom of the layout. An IntersectionObserver with rootMargin: loadMoreThreshold watches it, so the next request starts when the bottom is loadMoreThreshold px away from the viewport. After every page finishes the observer is subscribed again, which re-checks the current state: if the marker is still near the viewport (a fast scroll outran the content) the next page starts immediately. Raise loadMoreThreshold if users scroll fast or your API is slow. Make sure pageSize fills more than a screen. With very small pages the marker stays visible after each response and requests chain one after another. One request at a time A new request never starts while another is running. The guard is synchronous, so even a burst of triggers in the same frame results in a single request, and responses cannot arrive out of page order. When a request fails A rejected loadData is logged with console.error and automatic paging stops ( hasMore becomes false). This prevents a broken endpoint from being called in an endless loop while the marker is still visible. Choose how you want to recover: Remount the component with a new key to start again from page 1. Catch errors inside your loadData and return { data: [], hasMore: true } after your own retry logic, if you want paging to continue. Starting over when filters change The component loads page 1 on mount and never reloads by itself. When the query changes, remount it: TSX < VirtualMasonry key = { JSON . stringify ( filters ) } loadData = { ( page , size ) => fetchImages ( { ... filters , page , size } ) } renderItem = { renderCard } /> With DynamicMasonryView DynamicMasonryView calls page 1 itself to find the layout type and hands that response to the inner layout, so page 1 is requested once. Changing the controlled isMasonry prop remounts the inner layout and requests page 1 again. Unique items The library does not remove duplicates. If your API can return the same record on two pages (for example when new items are inserted while the user scrolls), de-duplicate inside loadData and keep key stable and unique.

h.t: Hand over a prefetched first page

x: What works on the server, what is deferred to the browser and how to hand over a prefetched first page. Add the use client directive The components use React hooks and are published without a directive. In the Next.js App Router import them from a client file: TSX "use client" ; import { VirtualMasonry } from "react-hybrid-masonry" ; export default function Gallery ( { first } : { first : { items : any [ ] ; hasMore : boolean } } ) { return ( < VirtualMasonry initialItems = { first . items } initialHasMore = { first . hasMore } loadData = { ( page , size ) => fetch ( "/api/images?page=" + page + "&size=" + size ) . then ( ( r ) => r . json ( ) ) } renderItem = { ( item ) => < Card item = { item } /> } /> ) ; } Hand over a prefetched first page Fetch page 1 in a server component and pass it as initialItems . The component then starts with that data, does not show the loading state and does not request page 1 again; the first loadData call is for page 2. TSX // app/gallery/page.tsx (server component) import Gallery from "./Gallery" ; export default async function Page ( ) { const res = await fetch ( "https://api.example.com/images?page=1&size=30" ) ; const first = await res . json ( ) ; return < Gallery first = { { items : first . items , hasMore : first . hasMore } } /> ; } initialItems is available on VirtualMasonry . DynamicMasonryView and FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry load their first page on the client. Hydration is safe Layout effects use useLayoutEffect in the browser and fall back to useEffect on the server. The container width is unknown during the server render, so the first render is an empty container on both sides and there is no hydration mismatch. Positions are computed right after mount, once the width is measured. What the server HTML contains Because positions depend on the measured width, the server HTML does not contain the cards , even with initialItems . If search engines must see the content, additionally render a crawlable list (for example links in the page, or a <noscript> block) next to the layout, or keep this gallery for content that does not need to be indexed. Loading it lazily The layout is only useful in the browser, so it can be split out of the initial bundle: TSX import dynamic from "next/dynamic" ; const Gallery = dynamic ( ( ) => import ( "./Gallery" ) , { ssr : false } ) ; Use this only when you do not need initialItems to avoid a loading flash.

The layout follows the container width. Here is how to control what it does at each size. How the width is measured The width of the layout container ( 100% of its parent) is read on mount and again on ResizeObserver notifications, window resize and visibilitychange . The extra listeners keep the layout correct when the window was resized while the tab was in the background. The state is only updated when the width actually changed. The parent must therefore have a real width. A hidden parent ( display: none ) renders nothing until it is shown. Waterfall: by width limits With minColumnWidth and maxColumnWidth the column count follows the width, see how the column count is chosen . This works well when you only need columns of a sensible size. Waterfall: columns per breakpoint When a design asks for an exact number of columns at specific widths, compute it yourself and pass columns : TSX import { useEffect , useState } from "react" ; function useColumns ( ) { const [ columns , setColumns ] = useState ( 2 ) ; useEffect ( ( ) => { const update = ( ) => { const w = window . innerWidth ; setColumns ( w >= 1600 ? 6 : w >= 1280 ? 5 : w >= 992 ? 4 : w >= 640 ? 3 : 2 ) ; } ; update ( ) ; window . addEventListener ( "resize" , update ) ; return ( ) => window . removeEventListener ( "resize" , update ) ; } , [ ] ) ; return columns ; } function Gallery ( ) { const columns = useColumns ( ) ; return < VirtualMasonry columns = { columns } gap = { 16 } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> ; } The same works for waterfallConfig={{ columns }} in DynamicMasonryView . Equal-height rows The equal-height layout has no column count: rows are rebuilt for every width by the same rule, so the number of images per row changes by itself. Adjust the look per breakpoint by passing different targetRowHeight and sizeRange , for example smaller rows on phones: TSX const small = window . innerWidth < 640 ; < FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry targetRowHeight = { small ? 140 : 245 } sizeRange = { small ? [ 120 , 170 ] : [ 230 , 260 ] } gap = { small ? 4 : 8 } loadData = { loadData } renderItem = { renderCard } /> Cost of resizing Every width change recomputes the layout of all loaded items. It is cheap for thousands of items, but avoid changing gap , columns or size options on every animation frame.

What the library does for you, and what to check in your own cards. What is already optimized Only items inside the viewport plus buffer are mounted; the rest of the list costs nothing in the DOM. The scroll position is updated at most once per animation frame ( requestAnimationFrame ). Item objects keep their identity while scrolling. They only change when items or the container width change, so memoized children do not re-render on every scroll. Layouts are cached with useMemo ; scrolling does not recompute positions. buffer buffer (default 1500 ) is the distance above and below the viewport that stays mounted. A larger value shows fewer blank areas when scrolling fast but mounts more cards and requests more images at once. A smaller value saves work but reveals the loading process on fast scrolls. Tune buffer and loadMoreThreshold while looking at the number of images requested and at your performance scores, do not just increase them until the picture looks better. loadMoreThreshold A larger loadMoreThreshold starts the next request earlier, which hides latency, but loads data users may never scroll to. Choose it according to your API latency and page size. Images Give every item its real width and height in the data. The layout is computed from them before the image loads, so nothing jumps when images arrive. Use loading="lazy" and decoding="async" on images, and serve thumbnails near the displayed size. Use object-fit: cover so a slightly different rounded size never distorts the picture. TSX < img src = { item . thumb } alt = { item . title } width = { item . width } height = { item . height } loading = " lazy " decoding = " async " style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" } } /> Cards Wrap the card in React.memo . Because item identities are stable, it re-renders only when its item changes. Keep renderItem cheap. Do not create observers or heavy state in every card; use a shared one where possible. Always set key={item.id} on the returned element. TSX const Card = React . memo ( function Card ( { item } : { item : any } ) { return ( < div style = { { position : "absolute" , left : item . x , top : item . y , width : item . width , height : item . height } } > < img src = { item . thumb } alt = { item . title } loading = " lazy " style = { { width : "100%" , height : "100%" , objectFit : "cover" } } /> </ div > ) ; } ) ; < VirtualMasonry renderItem = { ( item ) => < Card key = { item . id } item = { item } /> } /* ... */ / > pageSize Choose a page size that fills more than one screen including the threshold. Pages that are too small cause request chains; pages that are too large delay the first paint. 30 to 50 is a good starting range.

h.t: 2. Compute and clamp the row height

x: The row-filling algorithm, step by step. Useful when you tune `maxStretchRatio` and `sizeRange`. Input Every item has an aspect ratio r = width / height . Using the target row height H , the ideal width of an item is r * H . W is the container width and g the gap. 1. Build a row greedily Start a row with the next image. Before adding another image, compute the scale needed to make the current row fill the container: Text scale = (W - (n - 1) * g) / sum(r_i * H) // n images in the row If scale <= maxStretchRatio , the row is full enough: close it. Otherwise add the next image and test again. Adding an image always brings the scale closer to 1. If the row already needs to shrink ( scale < 1 ) it is closed as well, with no limit on shrinking. Because one image almost always needs a large enlargement to fill a row, this rule produces rows of at least two images without a special case. 2. Compute and clamp the row height Text rowHeight = H * scale rowHeight = clamp(rowHeight, minHeight, maxHeight) // sizeRange sizeRange is an independent visual density limit, so it is always applied. When the clamp prevents an exact fill, the next step makes the row end at the edge anyway. 3. Distribute widths without drift Each image gets r_i * rowHeight as its ideal width. To make the row end exactly at the container edge, the right edge of image i is computed from the cumulative share of the ideal widths, then rounded: Text available = W - (n - 1) * g rightEdge_i = (sum(ideal_0..i) / sum(ideal_all)) * available + i * g width_i = round(rightEdge_i - x_i) Rounding errors therefore never accumulate and are not pushed onto the last image, whose proportions would otherwise differ visibly from its real picture. Every width is then capped at maxItemWidth . 4. The last row The row at the end of the loaded data is not stretched ; its height is clamped between sizeRange[0] and targetRowHeight . If its natural width would overflow the container, all of its images are scaled down by the same factor. When another page arrives, the former last row becomes a normal row and is recomputed. 5. Virtualization Each item gets x , y , width , height and originalIndex . Only items that intersect the viewport extended by buffer are rendered, using the item's originalIndex as the React key. The total height minHeight of the container is the bottom of the last row. Tuning hints Many rows with 2 images means a large targetRowHeight for the container width: lower it or widen sizeRange . A very narrow sizeRange makes rows exact but allows only a few combinations; widen it if rows look uneven. Lower maxStretchRatio for less enlargement, raise it to close rows earlier.

Common questions and the usual cause of problems. Does it scroll inside its own container? No. It follows the window scroll and reads its own position with getBoundingClientRect, so put it in a normally scrolling page. Scrolling inside a nested overflow container is not supported. Items are stacked at the top-left or overlap each other. Why? The root element returned by renderItem must use position: absolute together with the given left, top, width and height. Without it the browser lays the items out as normal blocks. The container is tall but empty. Positions are only computed after the container width has been measured, so a container that is hidden (display: none) or has zero width renders nothing. Make sure it has a real width. Opening a hidden tab triggers a re-measure through visibilitychange and ResizeObserver. Why do I get duplicate key warnings or flickering cards in the waterfall layout? In VirtualMasonry the second argument of renderItem is the index among the currently rendered items, not the index in your data, and it changes while you scroll. Always put a stable key (for example key={item.id}) on the element you return. Loading stopped and never continues. Either loadData returned hasMore: false, or a page request rejected. A failed request sets hasMore to false so the library does not retry in a loop. Remount the component (change its key) to start again, or catch the error inside loadData and return an empty page with hasMore: true if you prefer to keep going. The same page is requested twice. Only one request is in flight at a time, so this is almost always React StrictMode running effects twice in development, or the component being mounted twice. In DynamicMasonryView the page-1 response used to pick the layout is cached and reused, so page 1 is not requested again by the inner layout. The layout does not switch when I change the API response. In uncontrolled mode the layout type is read once, from the first loadData call. Pass the isMasonry prop to switch at runtime. Switching remounts the active layout and loads from page 1 again. I get a hooks error in the Next.js App Router. The components use React hooks and are not marked with the use client directive. Import them from a file that starts with use client. Does enableAnimation do anything? Not at the moment. It is accepted for API symmetry between the components and reserved for later; items are positioned without a transition. Which fields are used as the item size? width/height, then w/h, then imgW/imgH. Use mapSize for any other field names. Items without a valid size cannot be laid out, so make sure every item has one.

Notable changes to the library. 1.1.0 Added VirtualMasonry : columns to fix the column count, initialItems and initialHasMore to start from a prefetched first page. DynamicMasonryView : waterfallConfig.columns . Server rendering support: layout effects fall back to useEffect on the server. Changed Equal-height layout: new row building rule driven by maxStretchRatio , widths distributed from cumulative ratios so rounding errors no longer end up on the last image, and the last row is scaled down uniformly when it overflows. Waterfall layout: the calculated column count never makes columns narrower than minColumnWidth . Fixed Quick scrolling could start two page requests at once; a synchronous guard now allows a single request. A failed request is no longer retried in an endless loop; paging stops until the component is remounted. Container width could stay stale after a window was resized in a background tab; resize and visibilitychange now re-measure it. Equal-height scroll position used a cached offsetTop ; it now reads getBoundingClientRect , so content above the list can change height safely. Visible items kept a stable identity while scrolling, so memoized cards no longer re-render on every scroll event. 1.0.1 First public release on npm : VirtualMasonry , FullWidthEqualHeightMasonry and DynamicMasonryView .
